title: Is AI Computing Power Becoming a Commodity?
gist: BCG argues AI compute is moving from opaque, flat-rate pricing toward a liquid, commodity-like market -- following Anthropic, OpenAI, GitHub, and Windsurf's 2026 shifts to metered pricing -- and estimates this shift could unlock up to $140 billion in annual 'dark value' via arbitrage (~$66B-$97B) and lower data-center borrowing costs (~$26B-$40B annually), using oil and power market analogies to map the benchmarks, indexed contracts, and derivatives needed to get there.

themes.theme: The end of flat-rate AI pricing

insights.claim: Anthropic began moving enterprise customers to a $20-per-seat base fee plus pay-per-token API rates in April 2026, explicitly tying the change to a deepening crunch in AI computing capacity.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Signals that compute scarcity is now being passed directly into enterprise AI budgets, making AI cost lines newly volatile for corporate buyers.
insights.locator: Anthropic began moving enterprise customers to a $20-per-seat

insights.claim: OpenAI moved its Codex product from flat-message pricing to token metering in early April 2026; days later GitHub tightened Copilot usage limits, and in March 2026 Windsurf replaced flat credits with hard weekly limits.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: A cluster of major AI tool vendors abandoning flat pricing within weeks of each other confirms this is an industry-wide repricing, not an isolated vendor decision.
insights.locator: Similarly, OpenAI moved Codex from flat-message pricing to token metering

insights.claim: The likely next step after metered pricing is dynamic token pricing, where inference prices move in real time with AI compute supply and demand -- similar to how wholesale electricity prices spike on hot afternoons and fall overnight.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Enterprises budgeting AI spend as a flat opex line should start planning for electricity-style cost volatility instead.
insights.locator: The next step in the market's evolution could be dynamic token pricing

insights.claim: Whether AI token pricing behaves like a liquid spot market or a sticky utility contract depends on substitutability: interchangeable workloads (e.g., a chatbot built on Claude, GPT, or an open-source model) support real price competition, while deep integrations such as custom silicon, fine-tuned models, or data-residency arrangements create switching costs that let providers price closer to negotiated relationship value than to marginal compute cost.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Buyers should push toward substitutable, model-agnostic architectures if they want to keep leverage over AI vendors as pricing becomes dynamic.
insights.locator: This market would work efficiently in a setting where models are substitutable

insights.claim: As dynamic pricing spreads, enterprises should schedule flexible, latency-tolerant workloads (batch jobs, model evaluations) to run when spot AI compute prices are low, use futures markets to hedge nonflexible-but-substitutable workloads, and scrutinize committed-capacity contracts to understand exactly what premium they are paying for vendor lock-in.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term action plan for enterprise IT/finance teams to reduce AI cost exposure before dynamic pricing becomes the norm.
insights.locator: Time flexible workloads strategically

themes.theme: Market scale and the $140 billion dark value opportunity

insights.claim: BCG projects the AI compute market will grow roughly sixfold, from $360 billion in 2025 to approximately $2.3 trillion in 2030.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Sets the scale against which all the dark-value and financing estimates in the piece are calculated -- a market this size makes even small percentage inefficiencies worth tens of billions of dollars.
insights.locator: BCG analysis projects that it will climb from $360 billion in 2025

insights.claim: BCG estimates that a shift toward a more liquid, transparent AI compute market could unlock as much as $140 billion in annual 'dark value' -- value trapped by inefficiencies in the supply and demand for capital, goods, and services that exists in virtually every industry.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: This is the article's central investable thesis: whoever builds or exploits the infrastructure that unlocks this value (benchmarks, exchanges, hedging desks) captures a multi-billion-dollar opportunity.
insights.locator: All told, BCG Institute estimates that this change could unlock as much as $140 billion

insights.claim: Applying BCG's general finding that 3%-4% of any industry's market size is capturable through arbitrage to an expected $2.2-$2.4 trillion AI compute market by 2030 implies $66 billion-$97 billion of annual arbitrage value.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Quantifies the pure trading/arbitrage slice of the dark-value opportunity, separate from financing savings.
insights.locator: BCG's dark value research, finds that 3% to 4% of total market size

insights.claim: The arbitrage opportunity splits roughly as $12 billion-$17 billion annually in AI chips (captured mostly by data center players), $22 billion-$34 billion in AI compute rental measured in GPU-hours (captured mostly by AI labs and large compute users), and $32 billion-$46 billion in end-user tokens (captured mostly by large enterprises).
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Tells investors which layer of the AI compute stack -- chips, rental, or tokens -- offers the biggest prize for which type of player, useful for positioning around exchanges, brokers, or hedging desks.
insights.locator: AI Chips. This segment could yield $12 billion to $17 billion

insights.claim: Geographic arbitrage of AI compute is often infeasible today because data transfer fees can erase savings and many workloads need real-time turnaround, but companies such as Lumen Technologies building high-capacity, low-latency networking for moving massive AI data sets could loosen this constraint over time.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Networking infrastructure buildouts (not just GPU supply) are a hidden enabler of AI compute market liquidity -- worth watching as a second-order beneficiary.
insights.locator: This constraint may become less relevant over time

insights.claim: Listed prices on AI compute providers' websites rarely reflect actual transaction prices, because AI labs and large users such as autonomous vehicle and biotech companies typically negotiate bilateral discounts, reserved-capacity deals, and enterprise agreements that go unreported.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Buyers currently have no reliable way to know if they're overpaying, which is exactly the gap a benchmark/index provider could monetize.
insights.locator: First, price discovery is limited

insights.claim: AI data center vacancy rates sit at just 1%, with roughly 92% of new capacity already precommitted before it is even built, reflecting a race among AI labs to lock up supply years in advance.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Confirms compute remains a genuine supply-constrained bottleneck, supporting continued capex and pricing power for data center operators in the near term.
insights.quote: roughly 92% of new capacity already precommitted before it is even built
insights.locator: This race to lock up supply is evident in data center vacancy rates of 1%

insights.claim: Despite near-zero vacancy and heavy precommitment, utilization on some GPU clusters that enterprises rent or own can be as low as 5%, according to Cast.AI -- though utilization is likely much higher at leading AI labs.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Reveals a large hidden pool of wasted, already-committed compute capacity that a secondary/resale market could recapture -- a direct source of the estimated dark value.
insights.locator: the utilization rate for some GPU clusters that enterprise users of AI compute rent or own can be as low as 5%

insights.claim: Per the Silicon Data H100 rental index, H100 GPU rental prices rose about 2.2% per month on average since January 2025, but with sharp volatility beneath that trend -- falling as much as 11% at one point and rising to roughly 25% above their starting level at another.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Quantifies the price risk that long-term bilateral contracts are currently trying (imperfectly) to hedge, and the volatility a futures market would need to price.
insights.quote: the price of an H100 GPU has risen about 2.2% per month since January 2025
insights.locator: According to the Silicon Data H100 rental index

insights.claim: H100 hourly rental rates swung from about $8 per hour at a peak in early 2024 down to $1.96 per hour by late 2025, then back up to $2.64 per hour by April 2026.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: A greater than 4x round trip in hourly rental pricing in roughly two years illustrates why GPU rental contracts are currently poor collateral for lenders -- the exact problem forward curves are meant to fix.
insights.locator: Rental rates in customer contracts, meanwhile, have been volatile

insights.claim: Emerging AI compute benchmarks such as the Ornn H100 Index and the Silicon Data H100 Rental Index use different data-collection and normalization methodologies, so the same GPU on the same day can show significantly different prices across indices -- unlike mature commodity markets such as oil, where differing benchmarks still converge on a common price view.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Today's AI compute 'benchmarks' aren't yet trustworthy enough to underpin derivatives -- an unmet need and potential opportunity for a dominant price-reporting agency to emerge.
insights.locator: But each benchmark uses a different methodology to collect data

themes.theme: Data center financing and the case for lower borrowing costs

insights.claim: AI data center loans today are secured by weak collateral: GPU hardware with uncertain residual value (new generations ship roughly every two years) and customer rental agreements that are volatile and often concentrated in just one or two counterparties -- pushing lenders toward tight loan-to-value covenants and high interest rates.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Explains why hyperscalers and neoclouds are currently paying elevated borrowing costs, and what specific risk (not just 'AI is risky') lenders are pricing in.
insights.locator: To understand why, consider the assets that secure data center loans today

insights.claim: Using LSEG/Refinitiv loan data (including a subset covering CoreWeave and xAI) and assuming $3.6 trillion of AI infrastructure investment from 2026-2030 at 70% loan-to-value, 4.5-year amortization, and SOFR at 3.6%, BCG estimates a reliable forward curve for AI compute could save data center players $116 billion in total financing costs, or about $26 billion annually.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: A concrete, modeled dollar figure for the financing benefit of building AI compute derivatives markets -- a hard number to anchor investment cases for exchanges or index providers.
insights.locator: To estimate the potential financing savings for data center players

insights.claim: If AI infrastructure investment reaches the high end of analyst projections -- $6 trillion from 2026-2030 -- the annual reduction in borrowing costs from a reliable forward curve could exceed $40 billion.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Shows the financing-savings opportunity scales directly with how large the AI capex cycle turns out to be, making it a leveraged bet on continued hyperscaler spending.
insights.locator: If AI infrastructure investment comes in at the high end of analysts' projections

insights.claim: Forward markets for both GPU residual value and rental rates would let data center players hedge hardware depreciation risk and rental-revenue volatility directly with financial counterparties, giving lenders the confidence to lower loan-to-value tightness and interest rates, freeing capital for more data center capacity.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific financial products (residual-value and rental-rate derivatives) that need to exist before cheaper AI infrastructure debt becomes possible.
insights.locator: The emergence of forward markets for both GPU residual values and rental rates

themes.theme: What oil and power markets teach about AI compute

insights.claim: Like crude oil, which varies by chemical composition, sulfur content, and origin, AI compute is heterogeneous -- but oil solved this problem through price reporting agencies that standardize bilateral transaction data into benchmarks like Brent and WTI, which represent only a small share of global output yet anchor pricing for the entire market.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Provides the template BCG says AI compute should follow: a small, trusted reference price can govern a much larger, messier physical market.
insights.locator: Like AI compute, oil is heterogeneous

insights.claim: Unlike oil, which moves easily via tankers and pipelines so a barrel in Houston and Rotterdam price within a few dollars of each other, AI compute is regional like electricity -- a GPU in Virginia is not interchangeable with one in Frankfurt because workloads must run where the underlying data resides.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Implies AI compute will never trade as a single global commodity like oil -- any exchange or index needs a regional design, closer to power markets than to crude oil markets.
insights.quote: a GPU in Virginia is not interchangeable with one in Frankfurt
insights.locator: AI compute differs significantly from oil in terms of portability

insights.claim: Power markets show three mechanisms keep even a regional commodity anchored to real costs: physical interconnection (flows from cheap to expensive regions narrow price gaps toward the cost of transmission), real-time price transparency published at every node, and financial markets letting traders arbitrage regional spreads without moving physical power. These mechanisms only work within connected systems -- isolated grids such as California and New Zealand can diverge freely.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Gives a precise three-part checklist (interconnection, transparency, financial arbitrage) for evaluating whether any given AI compute region will actually achieve efficient regional pricing.
insights.locator: Three enablers keep regional price differences anchored to real costs

insights.claim: The article's central market-structure prediction is that AI compute won't converge to a single global price, just as power doesn't, but it can still evolve into an efficient regional market complete with its own supply and risk-management tooling.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Sets investor expectations correctly: don't look for one global 'AI compute price' -- look for regional indices and regional hedging instruments instead.
insights.quote: AI compute won’t converge to a single global price, just as power doesn’t.
insights.locator: AI compute won’t converge to a single global price

themes.theme: Building blocks of a liquid AI compute market

insights.claim: Early market-making precedents already exist: Amazon Web Services launched EC2 Spot Instances in 2009 as a bidding market for unused capacity (later shifting to a model based on long-term supply and demand for spare capacity), and newer venues such as SF Compute have built GPU-cluster marketplaces with resale built in.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Shows the liquid-market model isn't purely theoretical -- working prototypes already exist and could be studied or scaled for the broader AI compute market.
insights.locator: Amazon Web Services, for example, launched EC2 Spot Instances in 2009

insights.claim: A mature AI compute market needs five building blocks: price reporting agencies producing standardized per-GPU-hour benchmarks; long-term contracts indexed to a benchmark plus a provider differential (e.g., 'OCPI H100 + provider differential', mirroring oil's 'Dated Brent + $2.50/bbl' structure) instead of multi-year fixed rates; financial derivatives (swaps, futures, options) tied to those benchmarks; cash settlement against the benchmark since physically moving GPU-hours is impractical (as ICE Brent and NYMEX WTI futures settle against Platts and Argus rather than physical delivery); and secondary markets, similar to airline seat resale, letting holders of excess reserved capacity resell it.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: A concrete product roadmap for anyone building AI compute market infrastructure -- benchmark, indexed contract, derivative, settlement mechanism, and resale venue, in that order.
insights.locator: An efficient and liquid AI compute market could include a number of valuable tools

insights.claim: Four structural headwinds are slowing this market evolution: AI compute's technical complexity (varies by time, hardware quality/generation, and geography, with hidden non-GPU costs like networking, orchestration, and support); lack of consensus benchmarks; still-ample equity capital for AI labs, which reduces urgency to manage price risk; and data center players' historical incentive to keep bilateral pricing opaque rather than standardize it, though some may now see transparency as a way to lower funding costs and win customers.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Tempers the bullish dark-value thesis with the reasons commoditization could stall or take years, useful for timing any related investment.
insights.locator: Technical Complexity

themes.theme: A stakeholder playbook for the transition

insights.claim: Recommended playbook for AI end users: tier demand into 'baseload' (customer-facing applications that must be served regardless of price) versus flexible workloads (batch summarization, internal research, report generation); hedge baseload exposure the same way companies hedge energy or foreign-exchange costs; and throttle, delay, or reroute flexible demand when prices spike.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: A direct action plan for corporate FP&A and IT teams to insulate earnings from AI compute price volatility.
insights.locator: Tier demand into separate baseload and flexible categories

insights.claim: Recommended playbook for AI labs and other large compute users: push for benchmark-indexed pricing (e.g., 'OCPI H100 + differential') instead of fixed rates on long-term commitments; actively manage exposure across the contract lifecycle (renewal cliffs, overage pricing, risk of being locked into above-market rates); arbitrage workloads across time, quality, and geography as switching costs fall; and route each workload to whichever provider/model offers the best price-performance rather than standardizing on a single vendor.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Because AI compute is often the single largest cost line for AI labs, multi-vendor routing and indexed contracts are presented as a strategic necessity, not a nice-to-have -- relevant to how frontier labs' margins evolve.
insights.locator: AI compute is the single largest cost line for most of these players

insights.claim: Recommended playbook for data center players: incorporate residual-value and rental-rate forward curves into loan underwriting (presenting lenders with forward-curve-based projections rather than bottom-up forecasts) to compress credit spreads, and hedge hardware depreciation and rental-rate risk directly with financial counterparties as derivatives markets develop.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Gives data center operators (and their lenders/investors) a specific mechanism -- forward-curve-based underwriting -- for realizing the estimated $26B-$40B in annual financing savings.
insights.locator: Use forward curves to lower financing costs

insights.claim: The article closes on the thesis that the era of opaque contracts and flat-rate pricing is ending, and that early movers -- whether end users managing cost exposure, data center players unlocking cheaper financing, or AI labs securing supply -- stand to capture disproportionate value as the shift unfolds.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/antti-belt
insights.so_what: Frames this as a first-mover-advantage moment across the AI compute value chain, not just a cost-saving exercise -- relevant to timing decisions on hedging tools, exchange participation, or vendor negotiation strategy now rather than later.
insights.quote: The era of opaque contracts and flat-rate pricing is ending.
insights.locator: The market for AI compute is changing quickly
